title:
Dong Zhuo burns the palace and slays the people
Sun Jian hides the jade seal and breaks his oath
paragraphs:
Now [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) whipped his horse up to the foot of the pass, but arrows and stones came down from the wall like rain, and he could not force a way in. The eight lords had [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and Zhang Fei in together to do them honor for the exploit, and sent a man to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s camp with word of the victory. Yuan Shao then sent written orders to [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) to bring up his army. Sun Jian took [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) and [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) with him to [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu)'s camp, and there, marking the ground with his staff, he said: "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) and I had no quarrel. Yet I have thrown myself forward regardless of my life and faced the arrows and the stones, to punish a traitor for the state, and to right the private wrong done to your own house. But you, General, give ear to slander and send out no grain, till I am beaten for the want of it. How could you!"
[Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu), abashed, had nothing to say, and ordered the man who had carried the slander to be cut down, to make his peace with [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian). Then word was brought in of a sudden: "A general from the pass has ridden into the camp and asks to see you." Sun Jian took his leave of Yuan Shu and went back to his own camp, and when the man was called in and questioned, it was [Li Jue](char-li-jue), a general whom [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) favored. "What do you come for?" said Sun Jian. Li Jue said: "The Imperial Chancellor honors no man but you. He sends me now to make a match between the houses. He has a daughter, and would give her to your son." Sun Jian flew into a rage and shouted: "Dong Zhuo flouts Heaven and knows no law, and he has overturned the royal house. I mean to destroy his kindred root and branch, and so make amends to the realm. How should I marry with a traitor? I spare your head this once. Go back quickly and give up the pass, and you shall keep your life! Delay, and your bones will be ground to powder!"
[Li Jue](char-li-jue) clapped his hands over his head and scuttled off like a rat, and came back to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) with the tale of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s insolence. Dong Zhuo was furious, and asked [Li Ru](char-li-ru) what should be done. Li Ru said: "[The Marquis of Wen](char-lu-bu) is lately beaten, and there is no fight left in the men. Better draw the army back to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) and move [the Emperor](char-prince-xie) to [Chang'an](loc-changan), and so answer the children's rhyme. They have been singing it in the streets these days past:
> At the western end, a Han;
> At the eastern end, a Han;
> Let the deer to Chang'an run,
> And the trouble shall be done.
As I read it, 'at the western end, a Han' answers to [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu), who flourished at the western capital Chang'an and handed the throne down through twelve emperors, while 'at the eastern end, a Han' answers to [Guangwu](char-emperor-guangwu), who prospered at the eastern capital Luoyang and has handed it down through twelve emperors now in his turn. The round of Heaven is come full and must turn back again. Move back to Chang'an, Chancellor, and there will be nothing to fear." Dong Zhuo was delighted. "But for your words I would never have seen it," he said. So he rode back through the night to Luoyang with [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu), to take counsel on moving the capital. He gathered the officers civil and military in the council hall, and said: "Han has had its eastern capital at Luoyang two hundred years and more, and the breath of its fortune is on the ebb. The vigor of the age, as I see it, lies now at Chang'an, and I mean to attend His Majesty on his journey west. Get your baggage ready, all of you, and lose no time."
[Yang Biao](char-yang-biao), Minister of the Masses, said: "The land within the passes is broken and desolate. To abandon the ancestral temple and forsake the imperial tombs with no cause will alarm the people. Nothing is easier than to stir the realm; nothing harder than to quiet it. I beg you to weigh it well, Chancellor." [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) said angrily: "Would you thwart the great design of the state?" Huang Wan, the Grand Commandant, said: "Minister Yang speaks rightly. In the old days, when [Wang Mang](char-wang-mang) usurped the throne, and again in the time of [the Gengshi Emperor](char-emperor-gengshi) and [the Red Eyebrows](misc-red-eyebrows), [Chang'an](loc-changan) was burned to a waste of tiles and rubble. The people were driven out of it, till not one or two in a hundred were left. To leave the palaces now for barren ground is not fitting." Dong Zhuo said: "The rebels are up east of the pass and the realm is tossed in disorder. Chang'an has Mount Xiao and Hangu Pass to guard it. It lies close to Longyou besides, so that timber, stone, brick and tile can be had at a day's notice, and the building of the palaces will not take above a month. Let me hear no more of this." Xun Shuang, Minister of the Masses, remonstrated: "If you will move the capital, Chancellor, the people will be in an uproar and have no rest." A great rage took Dong Zhuo. "I take counsel for the realm. What are the little people to me?" That same day he stripped Yang Biao, Huang Wan and Xun Shuang of their offices and made them commoners.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) came out and got into his carriage, and saw two men bowing toward it. He looked, and they were Zhou Bi of the Secretariat and Wu Qiong, Colonel of the City Gates. Dong Zhuo asked what their business was. "We hear you mean to move the capital to [Chang'an](loc-changan), Chancellor, and we came to speak against it," said Zhou Bi. Dong Zhuo rounded on them. "You two advised me to give [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) his office, and now he is in revolt. You are of one party with him!" And he shouted to his guards to thrust them out of the city gate and strike off their heads. Then he gave the order for the move, to begin the next day. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) said: "Money and grain are short just now, and there are a great many rich houses in [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) whose goods may be listed and taken by the state. As for the clients of Yuan Shao and his fellows, kill their kin and party and seize all they have. The gain will be past counting."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) sent out five thousand mailed horsemen to range the city and lay hands on the rich of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), some thousands of households in all. Flags were stuck above their heads, lettered large with the words Traitors and Rebels. They were driven outside the walls and killed to the last of them, their gold and goods seized. [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) drove the whole people of Luoyang, some millions of souls, out upon the road to [Chang'an](loc-changan), setting a troop of soldiers between every company of the common folk, so that they dragged and pushed one another along. Those who died in the ditches were without number. The soldiers were let loose besides upon men's wives and daughters, and robbed the people of their food. The noise of the weeping shook heaven and earth. Whoever went too slowly had three thousand men at his back to urge him on, naked blades in their hands, killing as they went.
Before he went, [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had fire set at every gate, so that the dwellings of the people burned, and the ancestral temple and the palace offices with them. The flames of the North Palace and the South ran together, and the halls and courts of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) lay all in ashes. He sent [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) besides to break open the tombs of the late emperors, with those of the empresses and consorts, and take the gold and jewels out of them. The soldiers took the chance to dig up the graves of officers and commoners till scarcely one was left. Then Dong Zhuo loaded gold, pearls, silks and all that was good upon some thousands of carts, carried off the Son of Heaven, the empresses and the consorts, and set out for [Chang'an](loc-changan).
Now Zhao Cen, one of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s generals, found that Dong Zhuo had abandoned [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) and gone, and he gave up [Sishui Pass](loc-sishui-pass). [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) drove his men in first, while [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) cut their way into [Hulao Pass](loc-hulao-pass), and the lords brought their armies in after them.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) meanwhile rode hard for [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), and saw from far off the flames going up to heaven and the black smoke lying along the ground. For two or three hundred li there was not a cock or a dog, nor the smoke of a hearth. He set his men first to putting out the fires, and bade the lords camp their companies on the waste ground. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) came to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and said: "Now that the traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has gone west, this is the moment to press the advantage and hunt him down. Why do you keep your men still, [Benchu](char-yuan-shao)?" Yuan Shao said: "The troops are all worn out, and I fear nothing will come of going on." Cao Cao said: "The traitor has burned the palaces and carried [the Emperor](char-prince-xie) away, and all within the seas is shaken and knows not where to turn. This is the hour Heaven has appointed for his ruin, and one battle will settle the realm. What do you doubt, that you will not advance?" The lords all said it would not do to move rashly. Cao Cao burst out: "These boys are not worth taking counsel with!" And he took above ten thousand men of his own, with [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun), [Xiahou Yuan](char-xiahou-yuan), [Cao Ren](char-cao-ren), [Cao Hong](char-cao-hong), [Li Dian](char-li-dian) and [Yue Jin](char-yue-jin), and rode through the night after Dong Zhuo.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), for his part, had come to the neighborhood of [Xingyang](loc-xingyang), where [Xu Rong](char-xu-rong) the Grand Administrator came out to meet him. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) said: "You have only just left [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), Chancellor, and we must look for pursuers. Let Xu Rong lay an ambush beside the fold of the hills outside Xingyang. If a force comes after us, let it pass clean by. When we have beaten them here, he can close the road behind and fall on them. Then those who come later will not dare follow." Dong Zhuo took the plan, and ordered [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) to bring up picked men and hold the rear as well. Lü Bu was on the march when [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s army came up with him. "As Li Ru reckoned!" said Lü Bu with a laugh, and drew his men out in line. Cao Cao rode forward and shouted: "Traitor! You have carried off [the Emperor](char-prince-xie) and driven the people from their homes. Where would you go now?" Lü Bu railed back at him: "You turncoat and coward, how dare you talk so!" [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun) leveled his spear, put his horse forward, and made straight for Lü Bu. They had not fought many bouts when [Li Jue](char-li-jue) came driving in with a force from the left, and Cao Cao sent [Xiahou Yuan](char-xiahou-yuan) in haste to meet him. Then the shouting rose on the right as well, and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) came up with another, and Cao Cao hurried [Cao Ren](char-cao-ren) out against him. There was no standing against three armies at once. Xiahou Dun could hold Lü Bu no longer and galloped back into his own line. Lü Bu brought his mailed horsemen down upon them, and Cao Cao's army was broken and ran back toward Xingyang. They came to the foot of a bare hill about the second watch, with the moon making it light as day, and only then did they gather up what was left of them.
They were just setting the pots to cook when shouting broke out on every side and [Xu Rong](char-xu-rong)'s ambush came out upon them. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) whipped up his horse and forced a way out, but ran full upon Xu Rong and turned to fly. Xu Rong fitted an arrow and shot him in the shoulder. Cao Cao rode for his life with the arrow in him and turned past the slope of the hill, where two soldiers lay hidden in the grass. They saw his horse come on and drove in both spears at once, and the horse went down. Cao Cao was flung out of the saddle, and the two of them seized him. Then a general came galloping up, cut down both footmen with his blade, dismounted and raised him up. Cao Cao looked, and it was [Cao Hong](char-cao-hong). Cao Cao said: "I am a dead man, brother. Save yourself!" "Quick, to horse!" said Cao Hong. "I will go afoot." "And what will you do when the rebels come up with you?" said Cao Cao. "The realm can do without me, but not without you." "If I survive this, I shall owe it to you," said Cao Cao, and got to horse. Cao Hong threw off his coat of mail, trailed his blade, and ran at the horse's side. They had gone on till past the fourth watch when a great river barred the road before them, with the shouting coming nearer behind. Cao Cao said: "My fate has brought me here, and I shall not get away alive!" Cao Hong pulled him down from the horse, stripped off his gown and armor, and carried him over on his back. They were barely on the far bank when the pursuers came up and shot at them across the water, and Cao Cao went on wet through. By daybreak they had made another thirty li and more, and rested a while under an earthen ridge. Then the shouting rose once more, and a body of horse and foot came after them. It proved to be Xu Rong, who had crossed the river higher up and followed them.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) was in this strait when [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun) and [Xiahou Yuan](char-xiahou-yuan) came flying up with a dozen horsemen, shouting: "[Xu Rong](char-xu-rong), do our lord no harm!" Xu Rong made for Xiahou Dun, and Xiahou Dun leveled his spear and met him. A few bouts, and the spear went through Xu Rong and brought him down from the saddle, and the rest of his men scattered. [Cao Ren](char-cao-ren), [Li Dian](char-li-dian) and [Yue Jin](char-yue-jin) came searching afterward, each with his own troops, and found them. At the sight of Cao Cao, grief and gladness mingled in them. They gathered the remnant, above five hundred men, and went back in company to Henei. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s army went on its way to [Chang'an](loc-changan).
Now the lords camped separately in [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) put out what fire was left in the palace and quartered his men within the city, setting his tent on the foundation of the Jianzhang Hall. He had his soldiers sweep the tiles and rubble out of the palace buildings, and every tomb that [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) had broken open was covered and closed again. On the site of the Grand Ancestral Temple he ran up a rough hall of three bays, and asked the lords in to set the spirit tablets of the sainted emperors there, and an ox, a sheep and a pig were killed in sacrifice before them. When the rite was done they all dispersed, and Sun Jian went back to his camp. That night the stars and the moon shone together, and he sat out under them with his hand on his sword, looking up at the heavens. He saw a white vapor spread wide through [the Ziwei enclosure](misc-ziwei-enclosure), and sighed, and said: "The emperor star is dim, a traitorous subject throws the state into confusion, the people are trodden into the mire, and the capital stands empty!" And when he had spoken the tears fell before he knew it.
A soldier standing by pointed and said: "There is a glow of five colors rising out of a well south of the hall." [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) had torches lit and men let down into the well to drag it, and they brought up the body of a woman. She had lain there long, yet the body had not rotted. She was dressed after the palace fashion, and about her neck hung a brocade bag. They opened it, and within was a small vermilion box fastened with a golden lock. Within that again lay a jade seal four cun square, the knob of it cut into five dragons twined together. One corner was wanting and had been pieced out with gold, and eight characters stood graven upon it in seal script: "Having received the Mandate from Heaven, long may he live and forever flourish."
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) had the seal, and asked [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) what it was. Cheng Pu said: "This is [the Heirloom Seal of the Realm](misc-heirloom-seal). The jade of it was found long ago by Bian He at the foot of Mount Jing, where he saw a phoenix roosting upon a stone. He carried the stone away and brought it to King Wen of Chu, and when it was cut open there was the jade indeed. In the twenty-sixth year of Qin the jade workers were set to cut it into a seal, and Li Si wrote these eight characters upon it in seal script. In the twenty-eighth year [the First Emperor](char-qin-shihuang) was on progress as far as Lake Dongting when a great wind rose and the waves with it, and the boat was all but overturned. He flung the seal into the lake, and the storm stopped. In the thirty-sixth year he was on progress at [Huayin](loc-huayin), and a man barred the road with the seal in his hand and said to the Emperor's retinue: 'Carry this back to [the Ancestral Dragon](char-qin-shihuang).' When he had said it he was gone, and so the seal came back to Qin. The year after, the First Emperor died. Ziying afterward gave it up to [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) of Han. Later, when [Wang Mang](char-wang-mang) usurped the throne, the Empress Dowager Xiaoyuan flung the seal at Wang Xun and Su Xian and broke a corner off it, and the corner was pieced out with gold. [Guangwu](char-emperor-guangwu) came by this treasure at Yiyang, and it has passed with the throne down to this day. Of late, I hear, when the Ten Attendants threw the court into disorder and carried [the young Emperor](char-prince-bian) out to [Mount Beimang](loc-beimang), the seal was missing on the return to the palace. Heaven bestows it on you now, my lord, and it must be your portion to mount the throne. This is no place to linger. Go back quickly to [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong) and lay your plans for greater things." Sun Jian said: "That is just what I was thinking. Tomorrow I shall plead sickness and go home." When it was settled between them, he charged his soldiers privately to let nothing out.
But it so fell out that one of the soldiers was a man of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s own district, and thought to rise by it. He slipped out of the camp that night and carried the news to Yuan Shao, who rewarded him and kept him secretly among his own men. Next day [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) came to Yuan Shao and said: "I have a small sickness on me and would go home to Changsha, and I come to take my leave of you." Yuan Shao laughed. "I know what ails you. It is [the Heirloom Seal of the Realm](misc-heirloom-seal)." Sun Jian turned pale. "What is this you say?" "We have called the people to arms against a traitor, to rid the country of a plague," said Yuan Shao. "The jade seal is the treasure of the court. Since you have come by it, you should hand it over to the chief of the alliance before us all, to be returned to the court when [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has been put to death. Now you hide it and make off. What do you mean by that?" "How should the jade seal come to be with me?" said Sun Jian. "Then where is the thing that came up out of the well at the Jianzhang Hall?" "I never had it. Why force me so?" "Produce it quickly, and spare yourself trouble." Sun Jian pointed to heaven and swore: "If I have indeed got this treasure and hidden it away, may I never die in my bed, but perish under sword and arrow!" The lords said: "[Wentai](char-sun-jian) swears it so, and surely he has it not." Then Yuan Shao called the soldier out. "When they were dragging the well, was this man by?" Sun Jian in his anger drew the sword at his side to cut the fellow down, and Yuan Shao drew too. "To kill this soldier is to flout me." [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang) and [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) behind Yuan Shao whipped out their swords, and [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) and [Han Dang](char-han-dang) behind Sun Jian had their blades out as well. The lords all came between them and stopped the quarrel. Sun Jian got to horse at once, struck his camp, and left [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). Yuan Shao in a great rage wrote a letter and sent a trusted man through the night into [Jing Province](loc-jing-province), to [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) the Inspector, bidding him stop Sun Jian on the road and take the seal from him.
Next day word came that [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) had followed [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), fought at [Xingyang](loc-xingyang), and come back beaten. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) sent to bring him into the camp, gathered the company, and set out wine to cheer him. As they drank, Cao Cao sighed and said: "When I first raised the great cause it was to rid the state of a traitor, and you gentlemen came in on the side of right. What I had in mind at the beginning was this. [Benchu](char-yuan-shao) should have brought the men of Henei down upon Mengjin and Suanzao. You gentlemen should have held Chenggao fast, taken the Ao granaries, and stopped the passes of Huanyuan and Dagu, so keeping the strong ground in your hands. [Gonglu](char-yuan-shu) should have led the [Nanyang](loc-nanyang) men to lie at Dan and Xi and go in by Wu Pass, and so shaken the capital districts. All were to keep behind deep ditches and high walls and give no battle, but make a show of more armies than we had, that the realm might see where the strength lay. So the loyal cause would have cut the rebel down, and all been settled at a stroke. But you hang back and will not go forward, and the hope the realm had of you is dashed. I am ashamed of it!" Yuan Shao and the rest had no answer to give.
When the company broke up, [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) saw that [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and the rest each had his own designs. Judging that nothing would come of them, he took his own troops away to [Yang Province](loc-yang-province). [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) said to [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei): "Yuan Shao is good for nothing, and sooner or later there will be trouble. We had best go home." So he struck camp and marched north, and at Pingyuan he made Liu Bei Chancellor of Pingyuan, while he went off himself to hold his ground and nurse his army. [Liu Dai](char-liu-dai), Grand Administrator of [Yan Province](loc-yan-province), asked [Qiao Mao](char-qiao-mao), Grand Administrator of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery), for a loan of grain. Qiao Mao put him off and would not give it, so Liu Dai broke into his camp with his men, killed him, and took the surrender of all his following. Yuan Shao, seeing them scatter each his own way, led his troops out of camp as well, left [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), and went away into the lands east of the pass.
Now [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao), Inspector of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province), styled Jingsheng, was a man of Gaoping in Shanyang and of the imperial house of Han. From a boy he loved to make friends, and he had seven men of name for his fellows, so that they were called in their day the Eight Worthies of [Jiangxia](loc-jiangxia): Chen Xiang of [Runan](loc-runan), styled Zhonglin; Fan Pang of the same commandery, styled Mengbo; Kong Yu of the Principality of Lu, styled Shiyuan; Fan Kang of [Bohai](loc-bohai), styled Zhongzhen; Tan Fu of Shanyang, styled Wenyou; Zhang Jian of the same commandery, styled Yuanjie; and Cen Zhi of [Nanyang](loc-nanyang), styled Gongxiao. To assist him he had [Kuai Liang](char-kuai-liang) and [Kuai Yue](char-kuai-yue), men of Yanping, and [Cai Mao](char-cai-mao), a man of [Xiangyang](loc-xiangyang). When he had read [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s letter, he sent Kuai Yue and Cai Mao out with ten thousand men to cut [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) off.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s army had just come up when [Kuai Yue](char-kuai-yue) drew out his line and rode to the front of it. "Why do you bring men to bar my road, [Kuai Yidu](char-kuai-yue)?" said Sun Jian. "You are a subject of Han," said Kuai Yue. "How come you to hide the treasure of the realm away for yourself? Leave it with us now, and you shall go free!" That angered Sun Jian, and he bade [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) go out and fight. [Cai Mao](char-cai-mao) swung his blade and came to meet him. A few bouts, and Huang Gai brought his mace round upon Cai Mao and caught him full on the mirror plate over his heart. Cai Mao wheeled his horse and ran, and Sun Jian took the chance and fought his way across the border. Then gongs and drums sounded together behind the hills, and [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) himself came up with his army. Sun Jian saluted him from the saddle. "Why do you believe [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s letter, [Jingsheng](char-liu-biao), and press a neighbor so hard!" "You have hidden [the Heirloom Seal of the Realm](misc-heirloom-seal)," said Liu Biao. "Do you mean to rebel?" "If I have it, may I die under sword and arrow!" "If you would have me believe you, let me search the baggage of your army." Sun Jian said in a rage: "And what power have you, to dare make light of me!" They were coming to blows when Liu Biao drew back, and Sun Jian put his horse to the gallop after him. The ambush sprang up together from behind the two hills, with Kuai Yue and Cai Mao coming on behind, and Sun Jian was hemmed in on every side. Truly:
> What gain have those who win the royal seal?
> It yields but war, and summons hostile steel.
How Sun Jian got away, the next chapter will tell.

versions.name: Cai Mao
versions.description: Serves [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) as an officer.

versions.name: Cao Cao
versions.description:
Style name Mengde. Grandson of the eunuch Cao Teng by adoption.
Has raised an army to bring down [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Cao Cao
versions.description:
Style name Mengde. Grandson of the eunuch Cao Teng by adoption.
Has left the lords and taken his own army into [Yang Province](loc-yang-province).

versions.name: Cao Hong
versions.description: Style name Zilian. A cousin of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao).

versions.name: Cao Ren
versions.description: Style name Zixiao. A cousin of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao).

versions.name: Cheng Pu
versions.description: Style name Demou. One of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s four generals; carries an iron-spined serpent spear.

versions.name: Ding Yuan
versions.description: Style name Jianyang. Inspector of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province). Killed in his own tent by his foster son [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu).

versions.name: Dong Zhuo
versions.description: Chancellor of State, and master of the court.

versions.name: Emperor Gaozu
versions.description: Personal name Liu Bang, founding emperor of the Han dynasty; rose from commoner origins to overthrow the Qin and establish the Han.

versions.name: Gengshi Emperor
versions.description: Personal name Liu Xuan. A member of the Han house whom the rebels against [Wang Mang](char-wang-mang) set on the throne. He reigned at [Chang'an](loc-changan) until [the Red Eyebrows](misc-red-eyebrows) drove him out of it.

versions.name: Emperor Guangwu
versions.description: Personal name Liu Xiu, founding emperor of the Eastern Han (also known as Later Han); restored the dynasty after the usurpation of Wang Mang.

versions.name: Emperor Ling
versions.description:
The reigning Han emperor at the novel's opening.
Died of illness.

versions.name: Empress Dowager He
versions.description:
Sister of the Grand General [He Jin](char-he-jin); mother of the [Prince of Hongnong](char-prince-bian). Of humble origin from a butcher's household.
Thrown from a tower by [Li Ru](char-li-ru).

versions.name: Gongsun Zan
versions.description:
Grand Administrator of Beiping.
A schoolmate of [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) from his student days.
One of the lords risen against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Gongsun Zan
versions.description:
Grand Administrator of Beiping.
A schoolmate of [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) from his student days.

versions.name: Guan Yu
versions.description: Style name Yunchang. One of [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s two sworn brothers.

versions.name: Guo Si
versions.description: One of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s commanders.

versions.name: Han Dang
versions.description: Style name Yigong. One of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s four generals; carries a great blade.

versions.name: He Jin
versions.description:
Grand General of Han. Born to a butcher's household, and raised to power when his sister became [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he).
Killed inside the palace by [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the Ten Attendants.

versions.name: Huang Gai
versions.description: Style name Gongfu. One of [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s four generals; carries an iron mace.

versions.name: Kuai Liang
versions.description: Elder of the two Kuai brothers, who serve [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) as advisers.

versions.name: Kuai Yue
versions.description: Style name Yidu. Younger of the two Kuai brothers, who serve [Liu Biao](char-liu-biao) as advisers.

versions.name: Li Dian
versions.description: Style name Mancheng. An officer of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s staff.

versions.name: Li Jue
versions.description: One of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s commanders.

versions.name: Li Ru
versions.description: Son-in-law and counselor to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Liu Bei
versions.description:
Style name Xuande. A distant descendant of the Han imperial house. The novel's central protagonist.
Sworn brother of [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei).
Major of a Detached Division and acting Magistrate of Pingyuan County.

versions.name: Liu Bei
versions.description:
Style name Xuande. A distant descendant of the Han imperial house. The novel's central protagonist.
Sworn brother of [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei).
Chancellor of Pingyuan.

versions.name: Liu Biao
versions.description: Style name Jingsheng. Inspector of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province), and a member of the Han imperial house.

versions.name: Liu Dai
versions.description:
Inspector of [Yan Province](loc-yan-province).
One of the lords risen against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Liu Dai
versions.description: Inspector of [Yan Province](loc-yan-province).

versions.name: Lü Bu
versions.description:
Style name Fengxian. Foster son of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo); killed his former foster father [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan).
Serves as Cavalry Commandant, General of the Household and Marquis of Wen.

versions.name: Prince of Hongnong
versions.description:
Previously Emperor Shao. Elder son of [Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling); his mother was [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he).
Deposed by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), and poisoned in the Yong'an Palace by [Li Ru](char-li-ru).

versions.name: Emperor Xian
versions.description:
Previously Prince of Chenliu. Style name Bohe.
Set on the throne by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at the age of nine.

versions.name: Qiao Mao
versions.description:
Grand Administrator of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery).
One of the lords risen against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Qiao Mao
versions.description:
Grand Administrator of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery).
Killed by [Liu Dai](char-liu-dai).

versions.name: Qin Shi Huang
versions.description: Personal name Ying Zheng. He conquered the warring states and unified all of China, and was the first ruler to take the title of emperor. His dynasty fell within a few years of his death, and Han rose in its place.

versions.name: Sun Jian
versions.description:
Style name Wentai.
Marquis of Wucheng and Grand Administrator of Changsha.
One of the lords risen against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Sun Jian
versions.description:
Style name Wentai.
Marquis of Wucheng and Grand Administrator of Changsha.

versions.name: Wang Mang
versions.description: Regent to a child emperor of Han, he took the throne for himself and reigned as emperor of his own Xin dynasty between the two halves of the Han.

versions.name: Wen Chou
versions.description: One of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s two chief generals.

versions.name: Xiahou Dun
versions.description: Style name Yuanrang. Cousin to [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) through the Xiahou house.

versions.name: Xiahou Yuan
versions.description: Style name Miaocai. Younger cousin of [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun), and cousin to [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) through the Xiahou house.

versions.name: Xu Rong
versions.description: Grand Administrator of [Xingyang](loc-xingyang), and one of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s commanders.

versions.name: Xu Rong
versions.description:
Grand Administrator of [Xingyang](loc-xingyang), and one of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s commanders.
Killed by [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun).

versions.name: Yan Liang
versions.description: One of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s two chief generals.

versions.name: Yang Biao
versions.description: Grand Commandant, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).

versions.name: Yang Biao
versions.description: Minister of the Masses, one of the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers).

versions.name: Yang Biao
versions.description: Stripped of his office by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) and made a commoner.

versions.name: Yuan Shao
versions.description:
Style name Benchu. Of the great Yuan house.
Marquis of Qi and Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai). Chief of the alliance against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Yuan Shao
versions.description:
Style name Benchu. Of the great Yuan house.
Marquis of Qi and Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai).

versions.name: Yuan Shu
versions.description:
Younger brother of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao); of the great Yuan house.
General of the Rear and Grand Administrator of [Nanyang](loc-nanyang).
One of the lords risen against [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo).

versions.name: Yuan Shu
versions.description:
Younger brother of [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao); of the great Yuan house.
General of the Rear and Grand Administrator of [Nanyang](loc-nanyang).

versions.name: Yue Jin
versions.description: Style name Wenqian. An officer of [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s staff.

versions.name: Zhang Fei
versions.description: Style name Yide. One of [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s two sworn brothers.

versions.name: Zhang Rang
versions.description: Chief of the Ten Attendants. Drowned himself in the river below [Mount Beimang](loc-beimang).

versions.name: Mount Beimang
versions.description: A line of low hills just north of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), long used as a burial ground.

versions.name: Bohai
versions.description:
A commandery of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province).
[Show on map](map:Bohai commandery)

versions.name: Chang'an
versions.description:
The old capital of Han, on the south bank of the Wei River far west of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) made it his capital at the founding of the dynasty.
[Show on map](map:Chang'an city)

versions.name: Chang'an
versions.description:
The old capital of Han, on the south bank of the Wei River far west of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). [Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) made it his capital at the founding of the dynasty. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) carried the court here from Luoyang and made it the capital again.
[Show on map](map:Chang'an city)

versions.name: Dong Commandery
versions.description:
A commandery of [Yan Province](loc-yan-province), with its seat at [Puyang](loc-puyang).
[Show on map](map:Dong commandery)

versions.name: the Han River
versions.description: The greatest of the Yangtze's tributaries, running southeast across [Jing Province](loc-jing-province) to join it.

versions.name: Huayin
versions.description:
A county on the north side of Mount Hua, on the road east from [Chang'an](loc-changan) to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang).
[Show on map](map:Huayin city)

versions.name: Hulao Pass
versions.description:
A fortified gate on the eastern road to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), in the foothills of Mount Song.
Historically the same stronghold as [Sishui Pass](loc-sishui-pass); the novel makes them two separate passes.

versions.name: Ji Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the northern plain.
[Show on map](map:Ji province)

versions.name: Jiangdong
versions.description: The land south of the lower Yangtze, in the east of [Yang Province](loc-yang-province).

versions.name: Jiangxia
versions.description:
A commandery of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province) on the middle Yangtze.
[Show on map](map:Jiangxia commandery)

versions.name: Jing Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the central south.
[Show on map](map:Jing province)

versions.name: Luoyang
versions.description:
Capital of Han at the novel's opening.
[Show on map](map:Luoyang city)

versions.name: Luoyang
versions.description:
Capital of Han at the novel's opening. Burned and emptied by [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) when he carried the court west to [Chang'an](loc-changan).
[Show on map](map:Luoyang city)

versions.name: Nanyang
versions.description:
A large commandery in the north of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province), south of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang).
[Show on map](map:Nanyang commandery)

versions.name: Puyang
versions.description:
The chief city of [Dong Commandery](loc-dong-commandery).
[Show on map](map:Puyang city)

versions.name: Runan
versions.description:
A commandery of [Yu Province](loc-yu-province), southeast of [Yingchuan](loc-yingchuan). Home of the great Yuan house.
[Show on map](map:Runan commandery)

versions.name: Sishui Pass
versions.description:
A fortified gate on the eastern road to [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), in the foothills of Mount Song.
Historically the same stronghold as [Hulao Pass](loc-hulao-pass); the novel makes them two separate passes.

versions.name: Xiangyang
versions.description:
A city on the south bank of [the Han River](loc-han-river), in the north of [Jing Province](loc-jing-province).
[Show on map](map:Xiangyang city)

versions.name: Xingyang
versions.description:
A city on the plain southeast of [Hulao Pass](loc-hulao-pass), near the south bank of the Yellow River.
[Show on map](map:Xingyang city)

versions.name: Yan Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the eastern plain, east of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang).
[Show on map](map:Yan province)

versions.name: Yang Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the southeast, reaching from the lower Yangtze to the southern coast.
[Show on map](map:Yang province)

versions.name: Yingchuan
versions.description:
A commandery of [Yu Province](loc-yu-province) southeast of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang), famed for the scholars it produced.
[Show on map](map:Yingchuan commandery)

versions.name: Yu Province
versions.description:
A Han province of the central plain.
[Show on map](map:Yu province)

versions.name: Heirloom Seal of the Realm
versions.description:
The jade seal of state, cut for [Qin Shi Huang](char-qin-shihuang) and handed down through the Han as the token of the Mandate of Heaven.
Currently missing from the palace.

versions.name: Heirloom Seal of the Realm
versions.description:
The jade seal of state, cut for [Qin Shi Huang](char-qin-shihuang) and handed down through the Han as the token of the Mandate of Heaven.
Currently in [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s keeping.

versions.name: The Red Eyebrows
versions.description: A rebel host of the years when [Wang Mang](char-wang-mang) fell, named for the red paint its men wore on their brows to tell friend from foe. They took [Chang'an](loc-changan), burned its palaces and plundered the city.

versions.name: Three Ducal Ministers
versions.description: The three highest-ranking civil officials of the Han court: the Grand Commandant, the Minister of the Masses, and the Minister of Works.

versions.name: the Ziwei enclosure
versions.description: The ring of stars about the north pole of the sky. The emperor star within it stands for the Emperor himself.
